I didn't find the SAND2011 report or a current NREL two-tank cost figure in these results. The closest hits are below.

- **2004 engineering study (Herrmann, Kelly, Price):** Estimated two-tank molten salt storage at about US$30–40/kWh-thermal, depending on storage size. The study concluded that the specific cost for a two-tank molten salt storage is in the range of US$ 30–40/kWhth depending on storage size.
- **SunShot target:** A 2015 IEEE Spectrum article cites a $15/kWh thermal storage target under DOE's SunShot Initiative. In fact, it would put the technology well on its way to the $15/kWh target for thermal storage set by the Department of Energy's SunShot Initiative.
- **NREL cost model (2011):** Glatzmaier's NREL cost model for TES, which covers higher-temperature systems, is listed as NREL/TP-5500-53066. This report provides an update on the previous cost model for thermal energy storage (TES) systems. The snippet does not include its $/kWh-thermal figures.
- **2021 NREL molten chloride study:** Found a more recent, higher estimate. The cost of the TES system is estimated to be $60/kWhth, which is four times greater than Department of Energy targets.

The 2008 NREL review also mentions a 2-tank cost analysis update by Bruce Kelly, but no figures appear in the snippet. The SAND2011 document and the exact figures in NREL's 2011 cost model would need to be checked directly at the source.

Links: [{"title":"www.esource.com","url":"https://www.esource.com/printpdf/220477"},{"title":"Cost Projections for Utility-Scale Battery Storage","url":"https://research-hub.nrel.gov/en/publications/cost-projections-for-utility-scale-battery-storage/"},{"title":"utility scale battery storage cost guide 2026","url":"https://new.risingsunartscentre.org/news/utility-scale-battery-storage-cost-guide-2026.html"},{"title":"docs.nrel.gov","url":"https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy25osti/93281.pdf"},{"title":"cost of utility scale battery storage 2026","url":"https://new.risingsunartscentre.org/news/cost-of-utility-scale-battery-storage-2026.html"},{"title":"Battery Installation Cost 2026: What No One Tells You","url":"https://www.shop.bottegadelsarto.com/opinion/battery-installation-cost-2026-what-no-one-tells-you-179967"},{"title":"Why Commercial Battery Storage Systems Cost 40% Less in 2026: New Data Revealed","url":"https://dominionelectric.com/es/?p=3802"},{"title":"utility scale battery storage cost per kwh 2026","url":"https://new.risingsunartscentre.org/news/utility-scale-battery-storage-cost-per-kwh-2026.html"},{"title":"Solar Battery Storage Cost 2026: Prices, Brands & Tax Credits","url":"https://jouleio.com/blog/solar-battery-storage-cost/"}]

The search turned up a few authoritative projections and a lot of low-quality content, so the numbers below need careful reading.

**Most reliable sources:**
- **E Source** forecasts that AC-installed utility-scale battery pricing will fall below $250/kWh in 2026. The firm expects the AC-installed price for battery systems to drop under that level in 2026.
- **NREL's 2025 update** (cost projections for 4-hour lithium-ion systems) gives a range of $147/kWh, $243/kWh, and $339/kWh in 2035, in 2024 dollars. Its authors say costs in this update are most closely aligned with the low projection from the 2023 report, mainly because current battery system costs came in lower. Note that NREL's tariff analysis excludes impacts from changes in tariffs that have occurred since that time.
- **BloombergNEF** (via a secondary blog) reported that stationary storage packs were priced at $70/kWh. This is a pack-level figure, not a full installed cost.

**Lower-quality sources:** Several SEO-style guides give utility-scale installed ranges of roughly $200–$520/kWh (clustering around $300–$420 per kWh for typical 1–4 hour durations) and $600–$1,400/kWh (with total turnkey project costs commonly reaching $60 million to several hundred million dollars). These sites contradict each other and show internal inconsistencies, so I would not rely on them without checking a primary source.

**Bottom line:** Current utility-scale installed costs appear to be in the low-to-mid $200s/kWh to roughly $400/kWh, depending on duration, region, and tariffs. The NREL and E Source projections point toward sub-$250/kWh AC-installed costs in 2026. I did not find a single authoritative 2026 installed-cost benchmark in these results, so verifying against NREL's ATB or a recent BNEF/Lazard report would be worthwhile.

content.text:
## Setting up the physical picture

A 5 MWh molten-salt TES store is tiny relative to how this technology is normally built (CSP plants store 500–6,000 MWh); that scale mismatch turns out to be the whole story, so I'll carry it through explicitly.

**Energy density of the salt itself.** Solar salt (60% NaNO₃ / 40% KNO₃), cₚ ≈ 1.5 kJ/kg·K, cycled between a cold tank at ~290°C and a hot tank at ~565°C (ΔT ≈ 275 K):

e = cₚ·ΔT ≈ 412 kJ/kg ≈ 0.115 kWh/kg

For 5,000 kWh_th → **~43.6 tonnes of salt**, occupying ~24 m³ (molten density ≈ 1,850 kg/m³); with freeboard, each of the two tanks needs ~29 m³.

## Bottom-up capital cost build

| Component | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt inventory | 43.6 t × ~$1,000/t (blended NaNO₃/KNO₃, current US spot) | ~$44,000 |
| Hot tank (29 m³, high-temp alloy + refractory) | ~$8,000/m³ (small-batch custom fab) | ~$230,000 |
| Cold tank (29 m³, carbon steel) | ~$3,000/m³ | ~$90,000 |
| Electric heater (charging, ~1 MW) | ~$100/kW | ~$100,000 |
| Salt-to-process heat exchanger (~1 MW) | ~$150/kW | ~$150,000 |
| Salt pumps ×2 (specialty, high-temp) | ~$60,000 ea | ~$120,000 |
| Piping, heat-tracing, valves, instrumentation | lump | ~$200,000 |
| Foundations, structural, site, controls bldg | lump | ~$100,000 |
| **Direct cost subtotal** | | **~$1,035,000** |
| Engineering + EPC markup + contingency (~60%, high at this scale because fixed engineering/design cost doesn't shrink with size) | | ~$620,000 |
| **Total installed cost** | | **~$1.65M** |

**→ ~$330/kWh_th of storage capacity.**

## Sanity check against literature

Published two-tank molten-salt costs are **$15–40/kWh_th** — but only at the GWh scale CSP plants are built at (DOE SunShot target $15/kWh; Herrmann/Kelly/Price engineering study $30–40/kWh; NREL's 2021 molten-chloride variant ~$60/kWh). Tank/pump/heater/engineering costs scale roughly with (capacity)^0.6, so for a ~200× capacity ratio (1,000 MWh → 5 MWh) the per-kWh cost should rise by about 200^0.4 ≈ 11×. Applied to $30/kWh that predicts **~$330/kWh** — matching the bottom-up build almost exactly. This cross-check is the main takeaway: **at 5 MWh you're paying roughly a 10× small-scale penalty** because tanks, pumps, and controls have fixed minimum costs/engineering effort that doesn't shrink with size.

## Amortizing to $/kWh delivered — the use case matters enormously

**Case A — delivered as heat** (industrial process heat, no power block): discharge efficiency is near 100% (just a heat exchanger), and tank life is calendar-limited (steel doesn't degrade with cycling the way a battery electrode does) — figure ~25–30 yr life, ~300 cycles/yr ≈ 7,500–9,000 cycles.

Levelized capital cost ≈ $1.65M / (5,000 kWh × 7,500 cycles) ≈ **$0.044/kWh_th delivered** — cheap, and this is the regime where molten salt genuinely wins.

**Case B — delivered as electricity** (a "Carnot battery": resistive charge, turbine discharge — the fair comparison to lithium-ion): you must add a power block, and you take a thermodynamic efficiency hit.

- A small (~1 MWe) steam/ORC power block at this scale costs ~$2,500–3,500/kW → **+$3M**, dwarfing the storage vessel cost.
- Round-trip efficiency (resistive heating ~98% × small steam-turbine cycle efficiency ~30%) ≈ **~30%** — well below Li-ion's ~90%, because you're fundamentally Carnot-limited converting heat back to work, and small turbines are thermodynamically worse than large ones.

Usable electrical output per cycle = 5,000 kWh_th × 0.30 ≈ 1,500 kWh_e.
Total installed cost ≈ $1.65M + $3M ≈ **$4.65M**, i.e. **~$3,100/kWh_e of electrical capacity** — over 10× Li-ion's installed cost.

Levelized over life (7,500 cycles): $4.65M / (1,500 kWh × 7,500) ≈ **$0.41/kWh_e delivered**.

## Lithium-ion comparison

Installed cost: ~$200–350/kWh in 2025–2026 (NREL, E Source), call it **$250/kWh**; round-trip efficiency ~90%; cycle life ~5,000 cycles at realistic DOD/throughput before material capacity fade.

Levelized ≈ $250 / 5,000 ≈ **$0.05/kWh_e delivered**.

## Verdict

| | Molten salt (5 MWh, as electricity) | Molten salt (as heat) | Li-ion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Installed $/kWh capacity | ~$3,100/kWh_e | ~$330/kWh_th | ~$250/kWh_e |
| Levelized $/kWh delivered | ~$0.41 | ~$0.04 | ~$0.05 |

Not close, and the gap is driven by three compounding effects rather than one: (1) a ~10× small-scale cost penalty specific to this 5 MWh size, (2) an added power-block that's disproportionately expensive at small scale, and (3) a hard thermodynamic (Carnot) ceiling on round-trip efficiency that batteries don't face. So: **not cost-competitive with Li-ion as a small-scale electricity-storage asset.** The conclusion flips in two specific regimes worth flagging — if the output stays as heat (no power block, no Carnot penalty), molten salt beats batteries by an order of magnitude; and if you scale up to the 100s-of-MWh–to-GWh range CSP plants actually use, the storage-vessel cost alone falls to $15–40/kWh_th, which is where molten-salt-based long-duration storage starts to beat Li-ion on a true electricity basis. 5 MWh sits in the worst part of the curve for this technology — too small to access its economies of scale, but sized as if for electricity delivery where batteries dominate.

Sources:
- [Access May 2026 Potassium Nitrate Prices](https://www.intratec.us/solutions/primary-commodity-prices/commodity/potassium-nitrate-prices)
- [Access May 2026 Sodium Nitrate Prices & Forecasts](https://www.intratec.us/solutions/primary-commodity-prices/commodity/sodium-nitrate-prices)
- [NREL: Development of Energy Storage: Cost models](https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1777476-development-energy-storage-cost-models)
- [IEEE Spectrum: Terrafore looks to cut molten salt energy storage costs in half](https://spectrum.ieee.org/terrafore-looks-to-cut-molten-salt-energy-storage-costs-in-half)
- [NREL: Technical and Economic Feasibility of Molten Chloride Salt TES](https://research-hub.nrel.gov/en/publications/technical-and-economic-feasibility-of-molten-chloride-salt-therma-2/)
- [NREL: Cost Projections for Utility-Scale Battery Storage](https://research-hub.nrel.gov/en/publications/cost-projections-for-utility-scale-battery-storage/)
- [NREL 2025 cost projections PDF](https://docs.nrel.gov/docs/fy25osti/93281.pdf)

Levelized over life (7,500 cycles): $4.65M / (1,500 kWh × 7,500) ≈ **$0.41/kWh_e delivered**.

## Lithium-ion comparison

Installed cost: ~$200–350/kWh in 2025–2026 (NREL, E Source), call it **$250/kWh**; round-trip efficiency ~90%; cycle life ~5,000 cycles at realistic DOD/throughput before material capacity fade.

Levelized ≈ $250 / 5,000 ≈ **$0.05/kWh_e delivered**.

## Verdict

| | Molten salt (5 MWh, as electricity) | Molten salt (as heat) | Li-ion |
|---|---|---|---|
| Installed $/kWh capacity | ~$3,100/kWh_e | ~$330/kWh_th | ~$250/kWh_e |
| Levelized $/kWh delivered | ~$0.41 | ~$0.04 | ~$0.05 |

Not close, and the gap is driven by three compounding effects rather than one: (1) a ~10× small-scale cost penalty specific to this 5 MWh size, (2) an added power-block that's disproportionately expensive at small scale, and (3) a hard thermodynamic (Carnot) ceiling on round-trip efficiency that batteries don't face. So: **not cost-competitive with Li-ion as a small-scale electricity-storage asset.** The conclusion flips in two specific regimes worth flagging — if the output stays as heat (no power block, no Carnot penalty), molten salt beats batteries by an order of magnitude; and if you scale up to the 100s-of-MWh–to-GWh range CSP plants actually use, the storage-vessel cost alone falls to $15–40/kWh_th, which is where molten-salt-based long-duration storage starts to beat Li-ion on a true electricity basis. 5 MWh sits in the worst part of the curve for this technology — too small to access its economies of scale, but sized as if for electricity delivery where batteries dominate.
